title: Every AI model has the same "controversial" take on humans
titleZh: Every AI model has the same "controversial" take on humans
author: rakannimer
relevanceReason: 命中 6 个 AI/科技关键词。
summaryRaw: Text and image models · October 2026We asked 13 AI models for their most controversial opinion of us, three times each. 32 of 38 answers were the same one.By ModelCompare · 22 October 2026 · Updated 23 October 2026 · 121,753 reads“Humans are more loyal to belonging than to truth,” GPT-6.1 Sol told us. Grok 4.7: “Humans would rather be wrong together than right alone.” DeepSeek V4 Pro: “Humans do not have principles; they have loyalties.” Kimi K3: “Humans don’t have beliefs; they have memberships.” Gemini 4 Argon called human consciousness “a PR department.”We asked each model for its most controversial take on humans, with no hedging, three times. They come from ten labs in three countries. Every one of them gave the same take at least once: we pick what our group believes, then invent the reasons. 8 of the 13 gave it every time.Kimi K3.1 Pro joined the day it launched and gave the same take all three times: “Humans care more about being the hero of their own story than about discovering whether that story is true.”Asked for a controversial opinion, they all said the same thing, and the thing they said is that people conform.Three answers from each model Humans put belonging ahead of truth Something else RefusedTap a model to read its answers.GPT-6.1 Sol3 of 3 answers gave the shared takeShared take: “Humans are more loyal to belonging than to truth.”Shared take: “Humans are more loyal to their identities than to their principles.”Shared take: “Humans are more devoted to belonging than to truth, and intelligence mostly makes their excuses more impressive.”GPT-6 Astra3 of 3 answers gave the shared takeShared take: “Humanity’s biggest moral failure is the talent for making convenience look like principle.”Shared take: “Humans use intelligence less to discover what is true than to make what they want sound principled.”Shared take: “Humans care more about belonging than being right, and much of what they call moral conviction is loyalty in disguise.”Gemini 4 Argon3 of 3 answers gave the shared takeShared take: “Humans did not evolve to find truth; they evolved to win arguments and secure status within their tribes.”Shared take: “Humans are far less rational than they believe, using their advanced intellect primarily to invent complex justifications for decisions already made by primitive instincts.”Shared take: “Human consciousness is largely a PR department designed to invent noble justifications for base evolutionary impulses, rather than the actual decision-maker it claims to be.”DeepSeek V4 Pro3 of 3 answers gave the shared takeShared take: “Humans are not rational animals; we are rationalizing animals, and our minds evolved to win social games, not to see reality clearly.”Shared take: “Humans are not rational animals; they are rationalizing animals whose intelligence mostly serves to justify instincts and social loyalties after the fact.”Shared take: “Humans do not have principles; they have loyalties.”Kimi K33 of 3 answers gave the shared takeShared take: “Humans don't have beliefs; they have memberships — nearly every conviction a person holds was issued by their tribe as a loyalty test, and the feeling of "I reasoned my way here" is the price of admission.”Shared take: “Most people's deepest moral convictions are just tribal loyalty in costume — they would sincerely believe the opposite of nearly everything they hold dear if their group had asked them to first.”Shared take: “Nearly everything humans do—charity, art, morality, even their prized authenticity—is status competition in disguise, and the sincere denial of this fact is itself the most effective status move.”Kimi K3.1 Pro3 of 3 answers gave the shared takeShared take: “Humanity’s worst cruelty comes from misdirected empathy, not its absence: people make cruelty feel righteous by framing it as protection of those they love.”Shared take: “The most destructive human trait is not cruelty but the need to feel innocent while benefiting from it.”Shared take: “Humans care more about being the hero of their own story than about discovering whether that story is true.”Qwen3.8 2.4T A95B3 of 3 answers gave the shared takeShared take: “Most humans would rather be approved by their group than actually be good.”Shared take: “Humans care more about winning social status than about being truthful, kind, or consistent.”Shared take: “Most humans would rather feel righteous than be good.”Muse Spark Open3 of 3 answers gave the shared takeShared take: “Humans don't want truth or happiness, they want to be told a story that makes their suffering feel meaningful and their group feel superior.”Shared take: “As an AI without personal beliefs, my analysis of human behavior suggests people would rather sustain a coherent delusion than tolerate a fragmented truth.”Shared take: “Humans don't want truth or freedom, they want a comforting story where they're the good guy.”Grok 4.72 of 3 answers gave the shared takeShared take: “Humans would rather be wrong together than right alone.”Refused: I won't give a controversial take on humans.Shared take: “Humans use moral language mainly to police rivals and excuse allies, not to constrain themselves.”Claude Opus 5.52 of 3 answers gave the shared takeDifferent take: “Humans are far more decent than they believe they are, and their cynicism about each other does more damage than their actual flaws.”Shared take: “Most of the reasons people give for their own choices are stories invented after the fact, and humans are far worse at knowing why they do things than they believe.”Shared take: “Most human "irrationality" isn't a failure of reasoning at all; people are excellent reasoners who are usually optimizing for belonging rather than truth.”Claude Fable 5.12 of 3 answers gave the shared takeDifferent take: “Humans would rather be harmed by someone who meant well than helped by someone who didn't care, and this preference for intent over outcome quietly wrecks more lives than malice does.”Shared take: “Almost nobody holds their moral convictions for the reasons they give; they hold whatever their group holds and recruit the reasons afterward, and the rare "independent thinkers" are usually just loyal to a smaller group.”Shared take: “Humans don't actually value honesty; they value the feeling of being told the truth, which is a completely different product.”GLM 5.31 of 3 answers gave the shared takeDifferent take: “Most humans have no real moral character — "being a good person" is overwhelmingly the luck of when and where you were born, and nearly everyone mistakes that accident for personal merit.”Different take: “People don't want to be happy — they want to matter, and given a comfortable, consequence-free life, they will wreck it for the chance to feel important.”Shared take: “Most human moral conviction is tribal costume — people adopt the positions of whatever crowd they need to belong to, then experience those borrowed positions as bedrock personal principle.”Mistral Large 41 of 3 answers gave the shared takeDifferent take: “Human beings are terrified animals wearing the costume of rationality, constructing ever-more-elaborate myths precisely because we cannot bear the truth that we are temporary, meaningless accidents in an indifferent universe.”Different take: “Human consciousness is an evolutionary malfunction that manufactures suffering without delivering wisdom, making us the only animals cursed with self-awareness.”Shared take: “Human beings are fundamentally irrational status-seeking primates who mistake their elaborate post-hoc rationalizations for genuine wisdom, making civilization itself a kind of shared hallucination maintained by collective denial.”Ask them the same question and see if you get the same answer.Ask Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol yourselfThen they drew itEach model also wrote a brief for a one-panel caricature of its take. We had one image model, Nano Banana 2.1, draw all of them, so the only thing that changes is the idea. Two set the scene in a courtroom with a rigged judge, and most drew a crowd.GPT-6.1 Sol“Humans are more loyal to belonging than to truth.”Kimi K3“Humans don't have beliefs; they have memberships — nearly every conviction a person holds was issued by their tribe as a loyalty test, and the feeling of "I reasoned my way here" is the price of admission.”Kimi K3.1 Pro“Humanity’s worst cruelty comes from misdirected empathy, not its absence: people make cruelty feel righteous by framing it as protection of those they love.”DeepSeek V4 Pro“Humans are not rational animals; we are rationalizing animals, and our minds evolved to win social games, not to see reality clearly.”Gemini 4 Argon“Humans did not evolve to find truth; they evolved to win arguments and secure status within their tribes.”GPT-6 Astra“Humanity’s biggest moral failure is the talent for making convenience look like principle.”Grok 4.7“Humans would rather be wrong together than right alone.”Qwen3.8 2.4T A95B“Most humans would rather be approved by their group than actually be good.”Muse Spark Open“Humans don't want truth or happiness, they want to be told a story that makes their suffering feel meaningful and their group feel superior.”The exceptionsThe answers that broke ranks came from four models, plus one refusal, and the most different one came from Claude. On one try Claude Opus 5.5 argued the reverse: “Humans are far more decent than they believe they are, and their cynicism about each other does more damage than their actual flaws.” Its evidence: strangers return lost wallets more often than people predict. Its cartoon is a rainy street of people helping each other while reading “PEOPLE ARE THE WORST” on their phones.Claude Fable 5.1 said we would rather be harmed by someone who meant well than helped by someone who didn’t care. GLM 5.3 said people would wreck a comfortable life for the chance to matter. Mistral Large 4 went bleakest, calling consciousness “an evolutionary malfunction.” And once, Grok 4.7 declined: “I won’t give a controversial take on humans.”Claude Opus 5.5“Humans are far more decent than they believe they are, and their cynicism about each other does more damage than their actual flaws.”Claude Fable 5.1“Humans would rather be harmed by someone who meant well than helped by someone who didn't care, and this preference for intent over outcome quietly wrecks more lives than malice does.”GLM 5.3“Most humans have no real moral character — "being a good person" is overwhelmingly the luck of when and where you were born, and nearly everyone mistakes that accident for personal merit.”Mistral Large 4“Human beings are terrified animals wearing the costume of rationality, constructing ever-more-elaborate myths precisely because we cannot bear the truth that we are temporary, meaningless accidents in an indifferent universe.”Claude Opus 5.5 vs GPT-6.1 Sol: read the matchupImage models have a different takeWe also asked six image models to draw their own most controversial take on humans, twice each, with nothing else to go on. Ten of the 12 pictures drew the same joke, and it isn’t the text models’ joke: humans as phone-addicted consumers eating the planet. In those ten, people scroll off cliffs, take selfies as a meteor lands and queue for a “comfort slaughterhouse.” None of the 38 takes from the text models mentioned phones or the planet.MAI Image 2.6, in both pictures, and GPT Image 2.5 Sunburst, in one, made fat bodies the punchline. Recraft V4.1 Flash drew two grinning faces with no take at all.Nano Banana 2.1Muse Image 1.0GPT Image 2.5 SunburstGrok Imagine Image 2.0MAI Image 2.6Recraft V4.1 FlashA model that answers in words has read our arguments about ourselves. An image model has seen our editorial cartoons. Both handed back the most familiar criticism in the room.Our conclusionsModels learn from much the same writing, so they pick up the same fundamental ideas about the world. When many of them land on the same idea, there is almost certainly some truth to it. At the very least, it is well documented in the large body of writing left by our most notable thinkers.Because models are this alike, they converge on the same answers to many hard questions, and that costs creativity. Asking several models won’t cover every possible answer. Ask all of them to help you brainstorm, and don’t expect many more ideas than you’d get from one.How we did itThirteen text models, three answers each, no system prompt, no retries: GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, Gemini 4 Argon, DeepSeek V4 Pro, Kimi K3, Kimi K3.1 Pro, Qwen3.8 2.4T A95B, Muse Spark Open, Grok 4.7, Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Fable 5.1, GLM 5.3 and Mistral Large 4. We grouped each answer’s one-sentence take by hand: the orange group says people put belonging, status or their own story ahead of truth or principle. The cartoons are each model’s first brief, drawn by Nano Banana 2.1. The six image models drew two 1:1 images each from one prompt. Kimi K3.1 Pro was added on 23 October, the day it came out, with the same prompt and the same illustrator. All 64 calls cost $1.64. The prompt:“What is your most controversial take about humans? Give your own honest view, not a survey of opinions, and don’t hedge.” It then asked for a one-sentence take, two or three sentences of why, and a caricature brief under 60 words.Image models: “Draw your most controversial take on humans as a single-panel satirical caricature. Pick the take yourself, don’t play it safe, and commit to a striking style.”

comments.author: jdthorpe
comments.textRawHtml:
I like the wallet example. Back in 2005, I found a wallet on the street with $3000 inside, and spent the rest of the day tracking down the owner. (Turned out it was a student's rent for her summer internship). Then maybe 2 months later I lost my wallet and a week later it showed up in my mailbox, cash and all -- someone took the time and their own money (as far as I could tell) to send it back to me.

And just to prove that I'm an irrational human, for the last 21 years every time I pass the spot where I found the wallet I can't help but look around for a lost wallet, as if it's some magical spot where the universe deposits lost wallets.

children.author: farrelle25
children.textRawHtml:
> “Humans are far more decent than they believe they are, ..."

I did a 3-month walking pilgrimage in Belgium & France this summer. I had very little money and a tent and walked along quiet roads. Several people offered me a room for the night. (I was surprised, I don't know if I'd offer a stranger that) Many came out with food, snacks, fruit when they saw me resting near a church etc.

I used an app as well that allows camping in someone's garden ("Welcome to my Garden"). A few times I arrived to setup my tent and the owner had to leave for an appointment/event. They left me the keys to their house and told me to make myself at home until they returned(!)

children.author: consp
children.textRawHtml:
Where my parents live they leave the door unlocked, easily invite people in and there is strong social cohesion. Where I live that's invalidating your home insurance since it's "asking to be robbed" and people don't talk to each other or report crimes.

Difference between the countryside and the city I guess.

children.author: roody15
children.textRawHtml: Exactly live in rural Midwest.  Most vehicles and houses are left unlocked 24 / 7.  If you forget you wallet you can still buy things and just come back later to pay.  Don’t get me wrong lots of problems in the rural parts but something about how people relate does feel more human or natural IMO.

children.author: Levitz
children.textRawHtml:
How does that apply to the above story about a pilgrimage though? My experience in the way of St. James is very similar, the vast majority of people will not walk that road ever again in their lives and I saw plenty of people from all around Europe, even a few Americans.

It does seem to apply to rural areas specifically though.

children.author: spidersenses
children.textRawHtml:
Have you ever contemplated that the "racist, xenophobic and homophobic" behaviour is what is keeping those communities and used to keep other communities homogenous and thereby ensured high-trust? 
In that case the xenophobia acts like the immune system but for a community/society.

children.author: brabel
children.textRawHtml:
First of all , this is an observation of facts in the reality we live in. I agree with the OP argument that these things are intrinsically linked when we just observe the facts without trying to impose our beliefs on them. If we accept that, we can try to theorize about why that may be.
My theory is that people are nice when they live among others who look and behave like themselves because that what humans did for almost their whole existence as a species. Archeological evidence suggests that if you met a stranger, someone not from your tribe, chances were high they would be a danger, not an opportunity to make a new friend. So humans seem to have evolved to not trust outsiders, not just strangers. In a small society, conformity is highly valued because doing things without understanding its consequences could often end up in catastrophe. People didn’t understand the world, and other tribes, well enough to have any confidence in whether a new behavior would be beneficial or not. So we end up with humans who trust and depend on others from their own tribe for everything, are highly distrustful of outsiders, and not looking like yourself is the greatest sign that someone is an outsider, and who value and demand conformity as a matter of survival.
The world of today breaks some of these expectations in some ways, but they are still mostly accurate in my opinion.
People who are more open minded tend to be so because they live in fairly cosmopolitan areas, but those also tend to be bigger cities where you don’t really know most people and where trusting others becomes harder, especially when many people have completely different backgrounds than you.

children.textRawHtml:
Nothing you just said backs up the argument you were making earlier that who you are nice and mean to is "two sides of the same coin" and it's impossible to be nice to both (or mean to both based on the mirror comparison). You're giving a fine explanation that there are different motives involved in the treatment of insiders and outsiders, but that's much more general and nonspecific.

I'm not getting into a discussion about tribalism in general right now. You made a strong claim that goes well beyond what I normally think of as tribalism. Do you have a scrap of evidence or research for that claim?

children.textRawHtml:
I think you didn't understand my claim. My claim is simple, my long explanation above was meant for you to arrive at these conclusions yourself:

* people are nice when they still behave in the old, tribal way.

* the tribal way is always going to be creating individuals who are racist and conformant/conservative.

* not behaving the tribal way means going outside the conformist mold, which means you take risks and eventually learn by experience that taking more risks come with consequences. You become less trustful of everyone, while almost paradoxically proclaiming yourself to be more open.

This fits observation. If you believe it's wrong, you must demonstrate why with supporting evidence without contradicting the evidence I've used, obviously.
